newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - Brent uneasy in sea of plenty.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - Brent uneasy in sea of plenty.

text.p: Benchmark Brent was likely to come under more pressure this week even without incremental Iraqi oil which the market had anticipated would begin to emerge in mid-month had the U.N. not frozen the oil-for-food plan.

By the Friday at least six Brent cargoes loading in the second half of September were homeless and moving in a slow trickle at increasingly lower levels. Dated Brent slumped from a premium of 24 cents to October paper early in the week to a discount of 5-10 cents by late Friday.
"At this rate, Brent is losing about five cents a day and apart from the rush of Forties cargoes which moved at the end of last week nothing has been done at all," a wet trader said.

With October cash Brent tracking the futures rally and selling at a 40-50 cent premium over September, shifting physical barrels will prove difficult next week despite positive margins, another trader said.
But he was more bullish, seeing the pattern of trading on the physical market as more speculative than based on fundamentals.
"It would be difficult to give reasons to go short, other than the plaintive cry that we are near year's highs," a trader for a European oil company said, citing lean stock levels.

"I think it is reasonably tight as far as North Sea availability goes. Statfjord will be out in October and the general feeling is that refinery turnarounds in both Europe and the United States are quite light so that would lead to a continuance of crude demand," the European trader said.

Several traders noted, however, that it was not a healthy sign when an equity producer bought a Brent cargo at October flat then a day later sold another at a 10 cent discount to October paper. That deal has not been confirmed.
One trader took three of the six Brent dates which turned wet on Friday afternoon. Only one date was clocked.

With the transatlantic arbitrage closed, market watchers feared that some of the Brent cargoes being hoarded by trading houses waiting for a window to open into the U.S. Gulf would reappear on the market this week and depress prices further.
Refinery margins improved last week. The Brent-gas oil spread gained more than 40 cents to $5.70 a barrel.
Sour crudes in the Mediterranean got a needed boost after sinking to levels which some sellers believed were overdone.
Russian Urals, which took over much of the Iraqi share in the Med after the 1990 embargo, improved more than 15 cents to trade at an 85 cent discount to Brent.
Traders said Urals could improve if loading delays at Novorossiisk persisted into this week. The main Black Sea oil terminal was shut on Friday.

The strength in gas oil was also seen supportive of sweet Algerian, Tunisian and Libyan crudes, which benefited from the strength in gas oil-rich West African grades, which would likely move into the Far East rather than into the Med.
